Yes. The story gives the June visit, a single day, scene-by-scene detail, so small exchanges about peaches, the bulb and the ice trays can build a texture of meaning. It then compresses three ordinary weeks into one brief paragraph (the heat, the borrowed fan, the stolen birdbath), which moves quickly to the crisis without losing continuity.

After the hospital scene, it slows down again. The quiet evening in the empty house lingers on details like the sprouted potatoes, the unused ice cubes and the newspaper stuck to the dresser. This lets the narrator's realization and grief build without being stated outright.

The contrast between expansive and condensed time matches what matters emotionally. It feels deliberate and well balanced.
